slides.title: Pressure, Winds, Storms, and Cyclones
slides.subtitle: Leaves swirl, doors slam, windows rattle, roofs fly off — the force of moving air shapes everything from a hurting bag strap to a 270 km/h cyclone.
points: Why are winds stronger on some days than on others?
Why are water tanks usually placed at a height?
Can air pressure really crush us?
What causes storms and cyclones — and if Earth stopped rotating, would cyclones still form?

slides.title: Pressure
slides.intro: Megha and Pawan carry equally heavy bags, yet only Pawan's hurts. The straps hold the answer — and lead us to define what pressure really is.

slides.title: Narrow straps dig in, broad straps don't
slides.body: Megha and Pawan carry **identical, equally heavy** bags to a picnic, yet Pawan keeps shifting his — it hurts his shoulders. The difference is the straps: his are **narrow**, hers are **broad**. The same weight spread over a **larger area** of the shoulder presses less. Since the area over which a force acts matters, we define a new quantity — **pressure**.

slides.title: Force per unit area
slides.body: Pressure is the **force acting on a unit area** of a surface — so **pressure = force ÷ area**. Here we count only the force acting **perpendicular** to the surface. Spread a weight over a bigger area and the pressure drops, which is exactly why a broad bucket handle and a cloth pad under a head-load both feel easier — they reduce pressure by **increasing the area**.

slides.title: Newton per metre squared, the pascal
slides.body: The SI unit of force is the **newton (N)** and of area the **metre² (m²)**, so pressure is measured in **N/m²**, also called the **pascal (Pa)**. Apply a force of **100 N** on a cardboard of area **2 m²** and the pressure is 100 ÷ 2 = **50 N/m²**.

slides.title: Everyday pressure at work
slides.body: When the area is **smaller**, the same force makes a **higher** pressure — which makes certain tasks easier. That is why we choose a sharp edge or a pointed end:
chips: Pointed end of a nail drives in easily
Sharp edge of a knife cuts the apple
Broad bucket handle eases the lift

slides.title: Do liquids exert pressure?
slides.intro: We know a solid weight presses on our shoulders. But does water in a vessel press too — and if so, does it push only down, or in every direction?

slides.kicker: ACTIVITY 6.1 · LET US TRY AND FIND OUT
slides.title: Two pipes, one bulge
slides.purpose: Does a **liquid** exert pressure — and does the bulge depend on the weight of water or on the **height** of its column? We compare two pipes of different widths to find out.
steps: Take two transparent pipes of the same length (about 25 cm) but different diameters
Tie a rubber balloon over one end of each, clamp them on a stand
Fill both pipes with water to the same level, about halfway
Observe whether both balloons bulge — and by how much
slides.observe: Both balloons bulge to the **same extent**, even though the wider pipe holds **more water**. So it is not the weight but the **height of the water column** that exerts the pressure — equal heights give equal bulges, no matter the width.

slides.title: Taller column, bigger bulge
slides.body: Pour **more water** into a pipe and the balloon bulges **more**. As the height of the water column rises, the **pressure at the bottom rises with it**. So the pressure a liquid exerts depends on the **height of its column** — which is exactly why **overhead tanks** are placed high: the tall column boosts pressure for a strong stream at the taps below.

slides.title: A bottle that leaks sideways
slides.purpose: Does a liquid press only on the **bottom**, or on the **walls** of its container too? We give water side-exits at equal height and watch where it goes.
steps: Take a plastic bottle and make four small holes near the bottom, all at the same height
Seal the holes with tape, then fill the bottle with water
Remove the tape from all holes at the same time
Watch how the water comes out
slides.observe: Water **spurts out of all four holes** sideways. So liquids exert pressure not only at the **bottom** but on the **walls too** — in fact, a liquid presses in **all directions**. This is why water fountains out of leaking joints in pipes.

slides.title: Where height puts pressure to work
slides.leftBody: Tanks sit high so the tall water column raises the pressure, giving a strong stream at the taps below — a tap on the first floor flows stronger than one on the second.
slides.rightBody: Water presses horizontally on the dam's walls, and this pressure is **largest near the bottom**. So a dam's base is built much broader than its top to withstand it.

slides.title: Pressure Exerted by Air
slides.intro: The air all around us is the atmosphere — and it is not weightless. Does this invisible blanket of air press on us the way water presses in a vessel?

slides.title: The atmosphere presses on everything
slides.body: The envelope of air surrounding Earth is the **atmosphere** — nitrogen, oxygen, argon, carbon dioxide and other gases, extending many kilometres up. This air is **all around us**, and like any matter it can exert a force. Does it press on objects? An activity with a paper plate will show us.

slides.title: Lift the covered plate
slides.purpose: Does **air** push down on a surface — and does that push depend on the **area** covered? We cover an inverted plate two ways and feel which is harder to lift.
steps: Invert a paper plate, fix a stick to it, and place it on a flat surface
Cover it with a chart-paper sheet folded twice (small area); lift with the stick
Now cover it with the same sheet unfolded (large area); lift again
Compare the effort needed each time
slides.observe: The plate is **harder to lift** under the **unfolded** (larger) sheet, even though the sheet's weight hasn't changed. Air pushes on the covering sheet, and the push **grows with area** — proving air exerts a pressure on all objects, the **atmospheric pressure**.

slides.title: Why air doesn't crush us
slides.body: Air over a **15 cm × 15 cm** area pushes with about **2250 N** — like the weight of a **225 kg** object. A rubber **sucker** sticks because, once you squeeze the air out, the **outside** air pressure beats the reduced pressure inside it. We aren't crushed because the **pressure inside our body** — from fluids and gases in our tissues — balances the pressure outside.

slides.title: Millibars and hectopascals
slides.body: The SI unit of pressure is **N/m²**, the **pascal (Pa)**. But meteorologists use a practical unit, the **millibar (mb)**, equal to **100 Pa**. Air pressure is also given in **hectopascals (hPa)** — and one hPa also equals **100 Pa**, so 1 mb = 1 hPa.

slides.title: Formation of Wind
slides.intro: Some days the wind blows hard, other days it is calm. Air escaping a balloon or a punctured tube always rushes one way — and that hints at what sets the whole atmosphere in motion.

slides.title: High pressure to low pressure
slides.body: When an inflated balloon is left open, or a bicycle tube is punctured, the air **escapes** — always moving from a region of **high pressure** to a region of **low pressure**. This simple direction of flow is the key to understanding how winds form.

slides.title: One balloon feeds the other
slides.purpose: Does air flow from high pressure to low — and does it stop once pressures are equal? We connect a full balloon to an empty one through a straw and watch.
steps: Insert one end of a straw into an uninflated balloon, sealing it tight
Inflate a second balloon, hold its mouth shut, and seal it onto the straw's other end
Release and predict what will happen to both balloons
Watch how their sizes change, and when the flow stops
slides.observe: Air moves from the **inflated** balloon (high pressure) into the **uninflated** one (low pressure) — the first shrinks, the second grows. The flow stops only when **both pressures are equal**. Moving air like this is **wind**: differences in air pressure set the air in motion.

slides.title: Heating drives the breeze
slides.leftBody: Land heats **faster** than water; the warm air over land rises, leaving **low pressure**, so cooler air blows **in from the sea** — a sea breeze.
slides.rightBody: At night the **sea stays warmer**; low pressure forms over the water, so the wind blows **from the land to the sea** — a land breeze.

slides.title: High-Speed Winds Result in Lowering of Air Pressure
slides.intro: People say high winds can blow roofs clean off. Two hanging balloons and a single breath between them reveal the surprising reason why.

slides.title: Blow between two balloons
slides.purpose: Does **fast-moving air** raise or lower the pressure? We blow into the gap between two hanging balloons and watch which way they move.
steps: Inflate two balloons of the same size and tie a string to each
Hang them from a stick with a gap of 6–10 cm between them
Blow air into the narrow space between the balloons
Note what happens — then blow harder and observe again
slides.observe: The balloons swing **towards each other**, and harder blowing pulls them together faster. Fast-moving air between them creates a **low-pressure** area, and the higher surrounding pressure pushes them in — so **high-speed winds are accompanied by reduced air pressure**.

slides.title: Low pressure above, higher pressure below
slides.body: When high-speed winds rush **over a roof**, the pressure above it drops below the pressure of the still air **inside** the house. If the difference is large and the roof is weak, it can be **blown away**. That is why it is safer to keep **doors and windows open** during such storms — letting wind through cuts the pressure difference and helps keep the roof on.

slides.title: Storms, Thunderstorms, and Lightning
slides.intro: Heavy rain, frightening thunder, sudden flashes of light — when high-speed winds meet rising moist air, a storm can crackle into a thunderstorm. How does it build, and what makes the lightning leap?

slides.title: From rising warm air to a flash and a boom
steps: Heating — warm, moist air rises, cooler air rushes in to replace it, and the circulation continues
Clouds — the rising air cools, vapour condenses into droplets that merge and fall as rain, hail, or snow; strong winds with rain make a storm
Charging — strong up-and-down winds rub water droplets against ice particles, so static charge builds in the cloud
Lightning — air's insulation breaks down, charges flow in a sudden flash, the air is heated and expands, and the boom we hear is thunder

slides.title: Charge splits, then leaps
slides.body: Positively charged **lighter ice particles** rise to the **top** of the cloud while negatively charged **heavier water droplets** sink to the **bottom**, separating the charge. The negative base also makes the **ground and trees** below turn positive. Air normally **insulates** these opposite charges — but once the build-up is huge, the air breaks down and **lightning** flashes within a cloud, between clouds, or between cloud and ground.

slides.title: What to do when lightning strikes
rows: Stay away from tall objects and trees
Find a low-lying area and crouch down
Crouch — do not lie down flat
Avoid metal-rod umbrellas; get out of water

slides.title: Local thunderstorms have local names
slides.body: Isolated, localised **pre-monsoon** thunderstorms appear across India under regional names — some helping kharif crops grow and fruit ripen:
chips: Mango showers — Kerala, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu

slides.title: The lightning conductor
slides.body: A **lightning conductor** is a metallic rod fixed along a building's wall during construction. Its **pointed top** is kept **higher than the highest point** of the building, and its other end is **buried deep** in the ground. The rod gives the electric charge an **easy path** straight into the earth, protecting the building from lightning.

slides.title: Cyclone
slides.intro: Over a warm ocean, rising moist air, released heat, and Earth's spin together build the most violent storm of all — a giant pinwheel of wind and rain with a strangely calm centre.

slides.title: How a cyclone is born
slides.body: Over **warm ocean water**, warm moist air rises and its vapour condenses into raindrops, **releasing heat** that warms the air further so it rises even more — driving an ever **lower pressure** as more air rushes in. **Earth's rotation** makes this in-rushing air **spin**. The whole spinning system of clouds, winds, and rain is a **cyclone**.

slides.title: Calm centre, violent ring
slides.body: The region of **lowest pressure** sits at the centre — the **eye of the cyclone**. At the eye the wind is **calm**, but the ring around it is lashed by **strong winds and heavy rain**. A cyclone gathers higher wind speeds than ordinary thunderstorms, and once it reaches land its source of moist air is cut off, so it **gradually loses strength**. The Amphan cyclone in 2020 reached peak winds of **270 km/h**.

slides.title: Damage and how to stay safe
rows: Storm surge 3–12 m floods the coast
Move early to a designated cyclone shelter
Track IMD weather reports and warnings
Salt water spoils crops and drinking water
Keep an emergency kit with essentials ready
Stay updated — satellites track the cyclone's path

slides.title: Words from this chapter
slides.body: The vocabulary of pressure and weather:

slides.title: Pressure runs the weather
slides.subtitle: From a sharp knife to a swirling cyclone, differences in pressure shape the air, the winds, and the storms above us — and knowing how they form is how we stay safe beneath them.
